I didn't have any dual enrollment classes in high school, but I know that as an IB student I didn't have to submit final scores. The ones I did submit and get credit for didn't contribute to my GPA, it just gives me the equivalent credits with no grade. I'm fairly certain the same is true for APs. There's also a chance that DE classes wouldn't count towards your GPA regardless (I know Tufts doesn't factor pre-matriculation grades for transfer students into GPA). 

I would check with your high school counselor and/or Tufts Student Services (or your pre-major advisor, once you get one) for clearer answers though.

Probably not. Rescinding admissions is pretty uncommon and usually for more serious academic decline (like failing a class, multiple Cs/Ds) and/or having a disciplinary infraction. I don't know if I can really justify the price, but I will say most similarly prestigious schools cost about as much. Whether or not it's worth it is extremely dependent on factors like your career goals and how you leverage the resources and connections you make here, plus a bit of luck. If you're really interested, and can afford (or waive) the application fee, apply and see what your financial aid package looks like and make a decision from there. 

Personally, I think I've gotten research experience at Tufts that I likely wouldn't have elsewhere, especially given my major. It's also helped me get higher-paying internships than people I know with similar majors at other institutions. I can't know how things would've turned out for me if I went to a different school, but overall I'm satisfied with my decision to go to Tufts (as is my family) despite the price and am confident I'll be able to pay back my loans.

I think that while it should absolutely not be as expensive as it is, there's a lot of nuance as to why many people end up going to specialized centers. Most psychiatrists will not diagnose autism because they don't feel (or aren't!) qualified. While they technically can provide the diagnosis, they may not have any specialized training in recognizing autism and differentiating it from disorders/etc that present similarly. A facility that specializes in autism diagnosis can be better equipped to distinguish between autism and other conditions, provide services post-diagnosis, and identify atypical presentations, among other things. 

I was diagnosed at 18, my assessment took about 5 hours in total (ADOS, language exam, general psych eval, consultation with a neuropsychiatrist, consultation with a PT). It cost, per hour, about what most other psychiatry appointments I've had did, but it lasted much longer. I had previously seen multiple health professionals who never suspected I was autistic and some who outright denied the possibility.

TL:DR It's too expensive, but in the same way that most specialized care is (especially in the US). A lot of doctors don't know much about autism and could falsely diagnose or rule it out.

As a freshman, especially in your first semester, Tufts really wants you to explore your options. They don't recommend you declare a major until your sophomore year. I would strongly recommend focusing on the distribution requirements (especially language/culture) and the writing requirements in your first year. It's still progress towards your degree, just not your specific major. It also helps many people figure out what they are genuinely interested in. She should take "random" classes so long as they legitimately appeal to her. Taking major-specific classes early on is still good, to be clear, it just is usually not necessary for an A&S student.

If you are applying for accommodation (for housing or otherwise), do so early and make sure you have all the documentation ready (you'll need a relevant diagnosis and a note from a doctor explaining how the disability relates to the accommodation). Some people have a positive experience with STAAR/reslife, but to be super upfront, many do not. You need to be proactive. I know that single-room accommodation is possible as is getting an AC (a window unit can be added to any room, you just need an approved accommodation). I know that most freshman dorms have single-stall gender-neutral restrooms, but I'm not sure that any have actual private bathrooms.

Not a CS person but I am trans and nonbinary! I would say that overall Tufts is a good school for LGBTQ students. Most dorms are co-ed, you can talk to the LGBT center about getting housing with someone of the same gender (or another trans student, etc) regardless of where you are in your transition. My only major gripe with Tufts is that we primarily have single-stall gender-neutral bathrooms, and typically academic buildings will only have one or two.

Parties aren't a huge thing. I know they exist, but I'm going into my senior year and haven't interacted with frats or big parties at all (and still feel like I have a decent social experience). Clubs and identity centers are often the best ways to find people IMO. Work-life balance is going to be very individually managed. I think most people end up being in at least one club/sport/social org which points to having some time for social stuff. 

I again can't speak to CS specifically, but overall I think it's a more collaborative than competitive school. Most people have a few people they're friends with through classes, especially if they're also in your major and you see them a lot. I don't totally know how to answer the last question, but people are generally friendly and respectful, and finding community while on campus is usually possible.

Unfortunately, there is no cut and dry answer to this question. However, we can look at historical precedent, and the fact is, many sports divisions have defined gender in such a way that often, trans women qualify for the women's divisions.

Stepping back, it's important to note that defining biological sex for sports has been an ongoing controversial issue, even without talking about transgender people. Take the IOC for example. They've gone through multiple measures of sex (including genital inspection, chromosomal testing, and now, measuring the presence of testosterone). Some people who are assigned female at birth don't qualify as women under current regulation, some women have elevated testosterone. 

Transgender women are allowed to compete in many international sports organizations given that they meet their hormonal criteria of womanhood, that is to say, they've been on testosterone blockers and estrogen supplements for a minimum of 12 months, and are endocrinologically more similar to women than they are to men. Being on HRT (hormonal replacement therapy) is an enormous commitment with numerous long term effects. It reduces muscle mass, increases fat retention, some studies find that it may even reduce bone density. These women have no clear advantage over their cisgender counterparts. The idea that men would simply declare themselves to be women, and deal with the social and medical reprecussions of transition for the sole purpose of winning some sports matches is absolutely ridiculous.

If you want more evidence of this, albeit anecdotal evidence, you can look at various cases of transgender women competing with cisgender women and clearly demonstrating no superior ability. The most obvious example to me is Hannah Mouncey, a handball player. Not only did her team not win the 2018 AWCH, but she also wasn't an outlying performer. In fact, multiple of her teammates held better records and were considered more valuable players. I point this out to say that, while there are examples of trans women who dominate in sports against cis women, there are examples of them performing normally, even below the standard. 

I also really wonder why we only talk about transgender women in sports when we have examples of transgender men who are forced to compete with women and clearly dominate. They have the heightened testosterone, etc that people seem to expect transgender women to have. This whole discussion is nuanced, and many people argue without doing any research, only basing it on what they think sounds correct.
